items.stem: A condition affects 2% of people. A test detects 95% of cases and gives a false positive for 10% of healthy people. Find P(condition | positive). (10 points)

steps.ask: P(condition | positive) = ? (3 decimals or a fraction)
Why is the answer so low when the test catches 95% of cases?
opts: False positives from the large healthy group outnumber the true positives about 5 to 1
Sensitivity and the false-positive rate are the same number

ow.1: Nothing is broken; the test behaves exactly as described.
ow.2: They are different: 95% is P(+ | condition), 10% is P(+ | healthy).
ow.3: 0.95 × 0.10 mixes the two branches and is not part of the calculation.

steps.sol: Healthy people are 49 times as common, so 10% of them (0.098) swamps 95% of the sick (0.019).

items.note: Bayes in three moves: a joint probability for each branch, add the branches that match the evidence, divide.

items.stem: Urn I holds 3 red and 1 blue ball; urn II holds 1 red and 3 blue. Flip a fair coin to pick an urn, then draw one ball. It is red. Find P(urn I | red). (10 points)

steps.ask: In one sentence: why is the answer above 1/2?
steps.sol: Red is three times as likely from urn I (¾ vs ¼), so seeing red shifts belief toward urn I.

items.stem: X takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E[X], E[X²], Var(X) and Var(5 − 2X). (10 points)
items.note: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X): the sign of a disappears when you square it.

items.opt: The exam asks you to use Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², not to derive it.

steps.ask: Write μ = E[X] and expand (X − μ)².

steps.sol: E[X²] − 2μ · E[X] + μ² = E[X²] − 2μ² + μ² = E[X²] − μ²
